strings.name: Graça Machel
strings.role: Former Mozambican education minister and advocate for women’s and children’s rights
strings.summary: Graça Machel is a Mozambican political figure and humanitarian advocate who led post-independence educational development and headed the UN study on the impact of armed conflict on children. She founded the Foundation for Community Development and the Graça Machel Trust and helped establish The Elders, extending her public work into child protection, women’s economic participation and peace.
strings.coverageNote: Information checked through 18 November 2026. The Nelson Mandela Foundation confirms her participation in a discussion following its annual lecture in Cape Town on 6 November. Institutional profiles currently list her as Deputy Chair of The Elders. Her University of Cape Town chancellorship was a historical appointment from 1999 to 2019.
strings.influence.rationale: Her sustained advocacy for children affected by war, education and women’s development has influenced international humanitarian policy through UN research and public action.
strings.facts.f1.label: Birth and education
strings.facts.f1.value: Born on 17 October 1945 in Mozambique’s Gaza region, she studied languages at the University of Lisbon in Portugal with scholarship support. This educational experience is recorded separately from honorary doctorates awarded later.
strings.facts.f2.label: Educational work in the independence movement
strings.facts.f2.value: She joined FRELIMO in 1973, taking part in the independence movement and working as a teacher. In 1974 she became deputy director of FRELIMO’s secondary school at Bagamoyo, Tanzania; educational work formed an important starting point for her public career.
strings.highlights.h1.title: Placing children affected by war on the international agenda
strings.highlights.h1.text: The UN study she led combined field visits, consultations across several regions and expert research, addressing child soldiers, displacement, disrupted schooling and physical and psychological recovery. Its emphasis on protection, recovery and social reintegration informed subsequent policy debates on children and armed conflict.
strings.highlights.h2.title: Supporting women’s economic participation and community development
strings.highlights.h2.text: Through the Trust and the Foundation for Community Development, she promotes women’s economic and financial participation, education, nutrition and community organisations. She is the founder; the Trust’s November 2026 announcement identifies Shiphra Chisha as its chief executive.
strings.timeline.t1.title: Joining the discussion after the Mandela Annual Lecture
strings.timeline.t1.text: At the Cape Town International Convention Centre, she joined Juan Manuel Santos, Muhammad Yunus and a youth representative in a panel discussion. Santos delivered that year’s annual lecture; the Foundation’s 9 November report confirms that she attended the 6 November event.
strings.timeline.t2.title: Founding the Graça Machel Trust
strings.timeline.t2.text: She established a nonprofit platform for African women and children, focusing on women’s economic and financial empowerment, education, nutrition and good governance. It advocates through networks and partnerships; its objectives and programme scope do not mean the underlying social problems have been eliminated.
strings.timeline.t3.title: Helping establish The Elders
strings.timeline.t3.text: She became a founding member of The Elders, joining other public leaders in peace, human-rights and development initiatives. In October 2018 she became Deputy Chair alongside Ban Ki-moon. This is a position in an independent nonprofit organisation, not a UN office.
strings.timeline.t4.title: Becoming chancellor of the University of Cape Town
strings.timeline.t4.text: She became the university’s first woman and first Black chancellor, serving until 2019. The university describes the chancellor as its titular head, whose responsibilities include graduation ceremonies and major external engagements, distinct from the vice-chancellor responsible for day-to-day administration.
strings.timeline.t5.title: UN publication of the study on armed conflict and children
strings.timeline.t5.text: The Secretary-General transmitted the study she led to the General Assembly as document A/51/306. She had been appointed an independent expert on 8 June 1994. The study covered several conflict regions, not only Mozambique; the report date is distinct from later meeting presentations or policy implementation.
strings.timeline.t6.title: Receiving the Nansen Medal
strings.timeline.t6.text: She received the Nansen Medal for her sustained support for refugee children’s welfare. It is a humanitarian honour associated with UNHCR and should not be confused with the Nobel Peace Prize or later honorary degrees.
strings.timeline.t7.title: Founding Mozambique’s Foundation for Community Development
strings.timeline.t7.text: She established the Foundation for Community Development (FDC) to support civil-society organisations, community capacity and post-war reconstruction. It is a separate institution from the trust she founded in her own name in 2010.
strings.timeline.t8.title: Joining Mozambique’s post-independence government
strings.timeline.t8.text: She became the first minister of education and culture, promoting wider access to schooling and literacy; her service as education minister continued until 1989. Educational development unfolded amid independence and war, and its outcomes should not be reduced to one person’s contribution or statistics with inconsistent definitions.
